Do smaller models bet as well?
directions.title: Do Haiku and Sonnet, as bettors, also beat always-50% on the published findings Opus scored?
directions.assumption_at_stake: Knowing which way new findings went is a property of the strongest model only.
directions.cheapest_test: The bettor's prompt and settings, unchanged, on Haiku and Sonnet, over round 1's 116 post-cutoff items and round 2's 92 template items; Opus's answers are the archive.
directions.models: claude-haiku-5-5 and claude-sonnet-5-5 new calls; claude-opus-5-5 from the archive (rule 12 met)
directions.odds_event: On round 1's 116 post-cutoff items, both Haiku and Sonnet beat always-50%: Brier 95% bootstrap upper bound below 0.25 for each.
directions.odds_rationale: Program 4 is 6 hits in 6 scored, its odds ran low (P1 reversed here), and Opus scored 0.163, well clear of 0.25; Sonnet very likely passes. Haiku is the risk: weaker priors and worse calibration could push its Brier above 0.25. Above the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md) for Sonnet, held near it for the Haiku conjunct.
directions.question: Can the smaller Claude models also tell which way a newly published finding went, or only the strongest?
known: The strongest model beat always saying 50% on 116 findings published after its training cutoff (76% right).
The smaller models were never tried as bettors.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about 60 cents to find out whether the two smaller Claude models can also tell which way newly published research findings went, as the strongest one could? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means both clearly beat a coin flip)?
engine_only: the pre-cutoff memory advantage (ss-b3) is smaller on Haiku than on Opus: engine odds 0.55
both pass on round 2's template items: engine odds 0.55 (correlated)
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Does the bettor beat always-50% on 60 more model-psychology findings, its weakest field in round 1?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The bettor's skill holds in the field it scored worst in, not just on average.
directions.cheapest_test: 60 post-cutoff model-psychology findings written by the template writer (no model), the bettor on Opus, Sonnet and Haiku (the ss-b1 audit's item 4).
directions.odds_event: On the 60 model-psychology items, the Opus bettor's Brier 95% bootstrap upper bound is below 0.25; Haiku and Sonnet reported.
directions.odds_rationale: Round 1's model-psychology items were its weakest field, and findings about models are where a model's priors may mislead it; template items give little context. But the field average was still near passing and 60 items is a reasonable n. Near the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: Can the model tell which way new research about AI models' own psychology went?
known: Research on models' own psychology was the bettor's weakest field in round 1.
The auditor named 60 more such findings as the check.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about 60 cents to find out whether the model can tell which way new research about AI models' own psychology came out, its weakest area so far? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it clearly beats a coin flip there too)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.short: Beat each field's own base rate?
directions.title: Does the bettor beat a predictor that knows each field's own rate of positive headline results?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The bettor's edge over the publication-bias baseline is more than knowing which fields report wins more often.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: round 1's 116 post-cutoff items; for each item, a baseline set to its field's headline rate, learned leaving that item out; paired Brier difference.
directions.models: archive: the Opus bettor's committed answers (no new calls; Haiku and Sonnet in ss-f1)
directions.odds_event: The bettor's Brier minus the field-aware baseline's has a paired 95% bootstrap upper bound below 0.
directions.odds_rationale: The bettor beat the flat publication-bias baseline by 0.068, a sizeable margin; a field-aware baseline is somewhat stronger, but fields are small (wide estimates) and leave-one-out shrinks its edge. About a coin flip, above the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md) given program 4's record.
directions.question: Is the model's edge more than just knowing which research fields usually report good news?
known: The bettor beat a rule that says 'papers report their method works' by a clear margin.
Some fields report positive results more often than others; that was not used by the rule.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend an hour of laptop time (free) to check, from saved data, whether the model's edge is more than knowing which research fields usually report good news? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it still beats a field-by-field guess)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Is the bettor's advantage on older papers memory? Pre-register the recognition split on round 3
directions.assumption_at_stake: The better score on pre-cutoff papers (ss-b3) is recall of those papers, not easier items.
directions.cheapest_test: On round 3's pre-cutoff items, code before scoring whether each rationale names or recalls the specific study; compare the pre/post gap on non-recognised items only (the ss-b1 audit's item 2).
directions.cost: $0 beyond round 3's bettor calls (about $0.30 for its pre-cutoff items)
directions.odds_event: On non-recognised pre-cutoff items, Brier(pre) minus Brier(post) has a 95% bootstrap upper bound below 0 (the advantage is not recall).
directions.odds_rationale: Disclosed: the ss-b1 audit's exploratory look on round 1 gave -0.027 [-0.073, 0.022], an interval spanning 0, which this session has seen. A new round with the split fixed in advance is a fair test, but that look suggests the residual gap is small. Well below the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: When the model does better on older research, is that because it remembers the papers?
known: The bettor scored better on papers it may have read during training than on ones it cannot have read.
Memory and easier items could not be told apart in that round.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about 30 cents, within the next round, to find out whether the model does better on older research only because it remembers those papers? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it still does better on older papers it shows no sign of remembering)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Round 3: does the bettor still win when the items are written by a model outside the Claude family?
directions.assumption_at_stake: The bettor's wins depend on items written by its own model family or by a word-swap template.
directions.cheapest_test: Post-cutoff items written by a local open-weight model (Qwen2.5-7B, no Claude), mechanical checks, the bettor on three models. Being prepared by another session as ss-b9 (items/local_writer.py, uncommitted at remap time).
directions.cost: about $1.10 (writer $0, local; bettor on Opus about $0.60, Sonnet and Haiku about $0.50)
directions.odds_event: On at least 60 post-cutoff items from the outside writer, the Opus bettor's Brier 95% upper bound is below 0.25 and it beats the up-word rule (paired upper bound below 0). (Remap draft; ss-b9's pre-registration may differ, logged, both odds kept.)
directions.odds_rationale: ss-b1's audit called a non-Claude writer the strongest open rival. A 7B writer's items may be noisier or leak direction words, which could help or hurt; beating the up-word rule on them is the harder conjunct. Program 4's record (6 of 6) argues up from the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md); the conjunct holds it at a coin flip.
directions.question: Does the model still win when the test questions are written by a different company's AI?
known: Round 1's questions were written by a Claude model, round 2's by a fixed word-swap rule.
The auditor named a writer outside the Claude family as the strongest remaining check.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about $1.10 to find out whether the model still beats a coin flip at predicting new research findings when the questions are written by a non-Claude AI? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means it still clearly wins and beats a simple word rule)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration

directions.title: Does the bettor still beat the 'which version flatters the paper' rater when that rater is asked three times and averaged?
directions.assumption_at_stake: ss-b6's narrow pass came from the bettor knowing results, not from the flattery rater being noisier.
directions.cheapest_test: The ss-b6 rater prompt twice more on all 92 items, averaged with the first rating; ss-b6's two-leg rule, unchanged (the ss-b6 audit's item 2).
directions.models: claude-opus-5-5 only (rule 12 reason: the rater must match the bettor's model and setting for the comparison to mean anything; the three-model bettor is ss-f1)
directions.odds_event: Against the three-rating average, both legs' paired Brier upper bounds are below 0 on the 92 items.
directions.odds_rationale: ss-b6 passed barely (flattery rule 90% right against the bettor's 93%), with the rater noisier than the bettor, the false-pass case D38 warned of. Averaging removes much of that noise; the audit's order-averaged check (d -0.050 [-0.086, -0.019]) says some gap survives. Near the running base rate 8/19 = 0.42 (ledger/brier.md).
directions.question: Did the model really beat a 'pick the flattering version' rule, or was the rule just noisy?
known: The model beat a 'pick whichever version flatters the paper' rater, but only barely.
That rater was noisier than the model, which can produce a false win.
directions.human_prompt: Would you spend about 90 cents to find out whether the model's narrow win over a 'pick the flattering version' rule survives when that rule is asked three times and averaged, so it is less noisy? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the model still wins)?
directions.odds_template: remap one pass (operators/remap.md), not v1; re-elicit under v1 before pre-registration
